scenarios.title: The service that won't stay enabled
scenarios.situation: You configured httpd to start at boot on a RHEL 9 server, but after every reboot the web service is down. You ran 'systemctl start httpd' last week and it ran fine. A colleague mentions the boot target might be involved, and you recall the unit file was modified recently.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct way to make httpd start automatically at boot, and how do you verify it?
evidence:
systemctl is-enabled httpd
disabled
systemctl get-default
multi-user.target
choices: Run 'systemctl enable --now httpd' to create the enablement symlink and start the service immediately, then confirm with 'systemctl is-enabled httpd'.
Run 'systemctl start httpd' after each reboot since the service works fine when started manually.
Edit /usr/lib/systemd/system/httpd.service directly to add WantedBy=multi-user.target under a new [Enable] section.
Run 'systemctl mask httpd' so systemd cannot override your manual start during boot.
scenarios.why: Starting a service and enabling it are separate actions in systemd: 'start' affects the current session only, while 'enable' creates a symlink in the target's .wants directory so it starts at boot. Never edit unit files under /usr/lib/systemd/system (package-managed); use 'systemctl edit' or drop-ins under /etc if customization is needed. 'mask' does the opposite of enabling.
scenarios.hint: Think about which command changes the state right now versus which one changes what happens after the next reboot.

scenarios.title: Port 8080 is open locally but unreachable
scenarios.situation: An internal app listens on port 8080 on a RHEL server. 'curl localhost:8080' works, but connections from other hosts time out. The firewalld default zone is 'public' and the app server is on the LAN where all internal hosts should have access.
scenarios.prompt: Which action most likely restores remote access without weakening security posture?
evidence:
firewall-cmd --list-all
public (active)
  services: ssh dhcpv6-client
ss -tlnp | grep 8080
LISTEN 0.0.0.0:8080
choices: Add the port permanently with 'firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=8080/tcp' then 'firewall-cmd --reload', so firewalld permits it in the active zone.
Stop firewalld entirely with 'systemctl stop firewalld' so nothing blocks the application.
Switch the default zone to 'trusted' with 'firewall-cmd --set-default-zone=trusted' to allow all traffic.
Add a rich rule dropping everything and re-install the firewall with iptables directly.
scenarios.why: The listener is bound to all interfaces, so the host firewall is the blocker — firewalld's public zone only allows ssh and dhcpv6-client. Adding the specific port permanently (plus --reload so the permanent config takes effect at runtime) is the least-privilege fix. Stopping firewalld or trusting everything removes protection far beyond this one port.
scenarios.hint: The evidence shows two facts: what the app is doing and what the firewall allows. Which one changes the smaller thing?

scenarios.title: Disk full at 60 percent
scenarios.situation: A RHEL file server reports 'No space left on device' while 'df -h' shows the /data volume at 60% used. The volume is LVM-backed ext4. A developer insists the filesystem must be corrupt and wants to reformat.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause, and what should you check first?
choices: The filesystem is out of inodes — a huge number of small files exhausted them. Confirm with 'df -i', find the directory with many files, and archive or delete them.
The LVM volume group is full, so extend the logical volume with 'lvextend' immediately.
The disk is failing — run badblocks and replace the drive before data loss.
The 5% reserved block count for root is too high; reduce it with tune2fs to free space.
scenarios.why: 'df -i' shows 100% inode use while block use is only 60% — a classic small-files exhaustion (mail spools, caches, session files). Reformatting destroys data unnecessarily. lvextend would add blocks, not inodes; reserved blocks only account for ~5%.
scenarios.hint: Blocks are the usual suspect, but there is a second resource every file consumes. The second command in the evidence names it.

scenarios.title: The web server SELinux denial
scenarios.situation: You moved a website's document root to /srv/www and updated httpd.conf accordingly, but browsers get 403 Forbidden. The error log shows permission denied. Files are owned by apache:apache with 755/644 modes, and the content was copied with 'cp'.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct fix?
evidence:
ls -Z /srv/www/index.html
unconfined_u:object_r:var_t:s0 /srv/www/index.html
ausearch -m avc -ts recent | grep httpd | tail -1
avc: denied { getattr } for comm="httpd" name="index.html" scontext=...httpd_t tcontext=...var_t
choices: Apply the proper SELinux type with 'semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/srv/www(/.*)?"' then 'restorecon -Rv /srv/www'.
Set SELinux to permissive in /etc/selinux/config so httpd is never blocked again.
Run 'chcon -R -t httpd_sys_content_t /srv/www' once — it persists across relabels.
Change ownership to root:root and chmod 777 so SELinux no longer checks the files.
scenarios.why: The files carry var_t (inherited from /srv) instead of httpd_sys_content_t, so httpd_t is denied access. 'semanage fcontext' writes a persistent file-context rule into the SELinux policy store, and restorecon applies it — surviving autorelabels and restores. 'chcon' alone is temporary and lost on relabel; disabling SELinux removes a whole protection layer for a labeling problem.
scenarios.hint: The AVC denial names the wrong type. The fix has two parts: declare what the type should be, then apply it.

scenarios.title: Rootless podman container can't bind port 80
scenarios.situation: A developer runs containers rootless with podman on RHEL 9. Their web container fails when publishing port 80, with an error about insufficient privileges. Running the same container as root works, but security policy forbids root containers.
scenarios.prompt: What is the best resolution consistent with rootless operation?
evidence:
$ podman run -d -p 80:80 myweb
Error: rootlessport cannot expose privileged port 80, ...
$ podman run -d -p 8080:80 myweb
<container starts>
choices: Publish an unprivileged host port (e.g. '-p 8080:80') and front it with a reverse proxy or firewalld forward rule to port 80; keep the container rootless.
Add the CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE capability to the container with --cap-add so rootless podman can bind port 80.
Run podman with sudo — rootful containers are the supported way to serve port 80.
Disable SELinux so the rootless port-forwarding helper is allowed to bind privileged ports.
scenarios.why: Ports below 1024 are privileged; an unprivileged user namespace cannot bind them, and --cap-add does not grant that across the user-namespace boundary. The standard rootless pattern is an unprivileged host port plus a proxy or NAT forward (firewalld rich rule) on port 80. SELinux is unrelated to the bind failure.
scenarios.hint: The kernel rule about low ports applies to the user, not the container. What sits in front of the container that already runs with privilege?

scenarios.title: Boot drops to emergency shell
scenarios.situation: After adding a new disk and editing /etc/fstab, a RHEL server drops to the emergency shell on boot. The journal shows the new mount failed. The admin is tempted to comment out the line and move on, but the disk holds production data needed at boot.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct recovery approach?
evidence:
journalctl -xb | grep -i mount
... Failed to mount /data.
... Dependency failed for Local File Systems.
blkid | grep sdb
/dev/sdb1: UUID="3f2a..." TYPE="xfs"
choices: In the emergency shell, verify the UUID with blkid, fix the /etc/fstab entry (UUID and xfs type), then 'systemctl daemon-reload' and 'systemctl default' to continue booting.
Comment out the line, boot normally, and mount the disk manually each morning.
Reinstall the OS — an fstab failure means the system is unrecoverable.
Run 'fsck' on the root filesystem; the failure is in the boot sequence, not the new disk.
scenarios.why: A wrong UUID, device name, or filesystem type in fstab is the classic cause — the emergency shell gives you a chance to fix it in place. blkid shows the real UUID; correcting the entry and continuing the boot preserves the production mount. Commenting it out just defers the outage; the root filesystem is not the problem here.
scenarios.hint: The journal says which mount failed. Which tool tells you the disk's true identity so the entry can be corrected?

domains.name: Users, Security & Services
domains.summary: EX200-weighted administration: password aging, ACLs, firewalld rich rules, SELinux booleans and custom policy, systemd timers, and journal persistence. Independent training content; this course confers no certificate.

scenarios.title: The Password That Never Expires
scenarios.situation: Audit flags 40 service accounts with passwords set to never expire. Policy requires 90-day rotation with a 7-day warning.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct enforcement?
evidence: Maximum number of days between password change: 99999
90-day max age, 7-day warn, applied to all human and service accounts
choices: `chage -M 90 -W 7 svc-deploy` (scripted across accounts) — chage sets max age and warning directly on the account aging fields
`passwd -e svc-deploy`; that enforces the 90-day policy
Edit /etc/shadow by hand for each account; chage doesn't work on service accounts
Password aging is cosmetic; the audit finding can be waived
scenarios.why: chage manages the shadow aging fields (max days, warn days, expiry) — the actual enforcement mechanism. `passwd -e` only forces change at next login. 99999 = effectively never, the classic audit finding.
scenarios.hint: Which command writes to the aging fields in /etc/shadow?

scenarios.title: Inheritance for New Files
scenarios.situation: The `releases` directory has the right ACLs today, but every file deployed tomorrow gets default permissions and breaks the pipeline.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct ACL setup?
evidence: group:deploy:rw- (effective) — but new files lack it
tomorrow's deploy artifacts are unreadable by the deploy group
choices: Set default ACLs: `setfacl -d -m g:deploy:rw /srv/releases` — default entries propagate to newly created files and directories inside
Re-run setfacl in a cron job every minute; ACLs can't inherit
Set the setgid bit; that propagates ACLs
Make the directory 777; inheritance problems disappear
scenarios.why: Default (`-d`) ACLs are the inheritance mechanism: new filesystem objects inherit the parent's default entries. Regular access ACLs apply only to existing objects. setgid affects group ownership, not ACL entries.
scenarios.hint: Which ACL variant applies to objects that don't exist yet?

scenarios.title: Forward, Don't Expose
scenarios.situation: A legacy app on port 8080 must be reachable as port 80 from the monitoring subnet only — without running anything as root on port 80.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct firewalld approach?
choices: A rich rule with forward-port scoped to the source: `firewall-cmd --permanent --add-rich-rule='rule family=ipv4 source address=10.20.0.0/16 forward-port port=80 protocol=tcp to-port=8080'` (+ masquerade if crossing interfaces)
Run the app as root on port 80; capabilities are overkill
Open port 8080 publicly and tell monitoring to use :8080
Use iptables directly; firewalld can't do port forwarding
scenarios.why: firewalld rich rules support forward-port with source scoping — port 80 stays unbound by any process while the firewall redirects. Running network services as root for privileged ports is the avoidable risk.
scenarios.hint: Which layer can redirect the port before any process binds it?

scenarios.title: The Boolean and the Custom Port
scenarios.situation: httpd must serve on port 8443 and connect to a remote database. SELinux blocks both: the port isn't labeled and the DB connection is denied.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct SELinux pair?
evidence: avc: denied { name_bind } for httpd on port 8443
avc: denied { name_connect } for httpd to db:5432
choices: Label the port (`semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8443`) and flip the boolean (`setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect_db on`) — ports need labels, cross-service connections need booleans
`setenforce 0`; two denials means the policy is wrong for this app
Run httpd as unconfined; booleans are deprecated
Add the port to the firewall; SELinux follows firewall rules
scenarios.why: SELinux has two independent gates here: port labeling (which ports a domain may bind) and booleans (which cross-domain connections are allowed). semanage makes the label persistent; `-P` makes the boolean survive reboot. The firewall is a different layer entirely.
scenarios.hint: One denial is about *binding*, the other about *connecting*. Which tool fixes each?

scenarios.title: audit2allow: Friend, Not Autopilot
scenarios.situation: A custom backup agent is denied reading `/data`. `audit2allow` suggests a policy module. The team wants to install it blindly.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct SELinux workflow?
choices: First verify the denial is legitimate (right domain, right target, expected access), then generate the module with `audit2allow -M`, review the .te file, and `semodule -i` — never install unreviewed policy, and check for a boolean or label fix first
Install whatever audit2allow suggests; it's the official tool so its output is always safe
Put the agent in permissive mode permanently; custom policy is unmaintainable
Relabel /data to backup_t; labels are easier than modules
scenarios.why: audit2allow translates denials into policy — including denials caused by mislabeled files or things that should never be allowed. Blindly installing it can codify a misconfiguration into policy. The workflow is: understand, prefer booleans/labels, then最小 custom policy, reviewed.
scenarios.hint: What does audit2allow know about whether the access *should* be allowed?

scenarios.title: Logs That Survive the Reboot
scenarios.situation: After a crash, the previous boot's journal is gone — `journalctl -b -1` shows nothing. The team needs post-crash forensics.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct journal configuration?
evidence: journal is in /run (tmpfs); lost on reboot
choices: Set `Storage=persistent` in `/etc/systemd/journald.conf` (creating `/var/log/journal`) and restart journald — the journal then persists across boots; also consider `SystemMaxUse` to bound disk usage
Copy /run/log/journal to disk in a shutdown script; persistence needs scripting
Set Storage=volatile; volatile means persistent in journald terms
Forward everything to rsyslog; the journal can't be persistent
scenarios.why: Storage=auto only persists if /var/log/journal exists; Storage=persistent creates and uses it. The default tmpfs-backed journal evaporates on reboot — exactly when you need it most. Bounding with SystemMaxUse/MaxFileSec prevents disk exhaustion.
scenarios.hint: Where does the journal live by default, and what kind of filesystem is that?

domains.name: RHCSA Spine: Boot, Storage, Networking
domains.summary: The core RHCSA admin spine — boot process, LVM storage, and networking troubleshooting on RHEL. Taught independently; this course confers no certificate and is not affiliated with Red Hat.

scenarios.title: Where did the boot stop?
scenarios.situation: A RHEL server hangs during boot with no login prompt. You need to determine whether it's a bootloader, kernel, or systemd-stage problem before choosing a recovery method.
scenarios.prompt: How do you localize the failure?
evidence:
GRUB menu displayed -> kernel selected -> messages scroll -> stops at:
[ OK ] Reached target Basic System
(no further output, no login)
choices: The boot passed GRUB and the kernel (messages scrolled, basic target reached), so the failure is in late systemd — boot with 'systemd.unit=rescue.target' from the GRUB command line to get a shell and inspect.
Reinstall GRUB — the bootloader must be corrupt since boot never finishes.
The kernel is panicking — boot an older kernel from the GRUB menu.
Replace the disk — hangs during boot always mean hardware failure.
scenarios.why: Boot stages are sequential: GRUB → kernel → systemd. Reaching 'Basic System' proves the bootloader and kernel worked; the hang is in later systemd units. The GRUB edit to add systemd.unit=rescue.target gives a root shell to inspect failed units with 'systemctl --failed'. Reinstalling GRUB or swapping kernels targets stages that demonstrably worked.
scenarios.hint: Each stage's success is proven by what you see on screen. What did the console prove already worked?

scenarios.title: Extend the volume, feed the app
scenarios.situation: The /var logical volume is at 95% and the app will halt at 100%. Free space exists in the volume group. This is ext4... no wait, check first — you must confirm the filesystem type before growing.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct sequence?
evidence:
vgs
  VG   #PV #LV  VFree
  vg_sys 2   4    20.00g
df -T /var
/dev/mapper/vg_sys-lv_var xfs  95% /var
choices: Extend the LV and grow the filesystem in one step: 'lvextend -r -L +10G /dev/vg_sys/lv_var' — the -r flag grows the xfs filesystem online automatically.
Run 'resize2fs' on the LV since that's the standard grow command.
Add a new disk to the VG first — you can't extend without new hardware.
Unmount /var, extend, remount — growing requires downtime.
scenarios.why: 'lvextend -r' extends the logical volume and then calls the right filesystem grow tool (xfs_growfs for XFS) while mounted — XFS only grows, never shrinks, and grows online. resize2fs is for ext4 and would fail on XFS. The VG already has 20G free, so no new disk is needed.
scenarios.hint: The evidence names the filesystem type. Which grow tool matches XFS, and can it run online?

scenarios.title: Two NICs, one confusion
scenarios.situation: A server has two interfaces: ens192 (management, 10.0.0.0/24) and ens224 (storage, 192.168.50.0/24). After a reboot, storage traffic is trying to go out the management interface and timing out.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause and fix?
evidence:
ip route
default via 10.0.0.1 dev ens192
default via 192.168.50.1 dev ens224 metric 200
ip -s link show ens224 | head -3
... state UP
choices: Two default routes exist — remove the storage interface's default gateway (set 'never-default' / no gateway on ens224) so only the management default remains, keeping the 192.168.50.0/24 route for storage traffic.
Delete the management default route so storage becomes the only path.
Bond the two NICs together so traffic uses whichever is up.
Assign both interfaces addresses in the same subnet to simplify routing.
scenarios.why: A host should have one default route; the second default on ens224 (higher metric, so backup) creates asymmetric/ambiguous routing for non-local traffic. Storage traffic to 192.168.50.0/24 uses the connected route regardless — it never needed a default gateway. Removing the spurious default restores deterministic routing.
scenarios.hint: Storage hosts are reached via the connected subnet route. What is a default gateway on that interface actually for?

scenarios.title: The snapshot before the upgrade
scenarios.situation: You're about to run a major package upgrade on a production RHEL host with LVM. The change window is 30 minutes and rollback must be possible if the upgrade breaks the app.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct safety procedure?
evidence:
lvs
  lv_root vg_sys -wi-ao---- 20.00g
  lv_var  vg_sys -wi-ao---- 30.00g
# VG has 15G free
choices: Create LVM snapshots of the root (and var) LVs before upgrading; if the upgrade fails, merge the snapshots back to restore the exact pre-upgrade state.
Copy /etc to /root/etc-backup — config files are all that matter.
Run the upgrade with '--skip-broken' so it can't fail.
Take a screenshot of 'rpm -qa' so you know what was installed.
scenarios.why: LVM snapshots are copy-on-write point-in-time images of the whole LV — 'lvcreate -s' before the change, 'lvconvert --merge' to roll back. A config backup can't restore binaries and libraries; --skip-broken just skips problems; a package list doesn't restore state.
scenarios.hint: Rollback means restoring the entire system state, not just configs. What LVM feature captures a whole volume instantly?

scenarios.title: GRUB password vs disk encryption
scenarios.situation: A security review of bare-metal RHEL servers in a colo: an attacker with physical access could boot into single-user mode via GRUB and get a root shell. The team debates mitigations.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct layered answer?
evidence:
Finding: physical access -> GRUB edit -> 'init=/bin/bash' -> root shell
Proposed: set a GRUB password
choices: Set a GRUB password AND encrypt data-at-rest (LUKS): the GRUB password blocks trivial boot-parameter edits, while LUKS protects data if disks are removed — neither alone covers both vectors.
A GRUB password alone is sufficient — it stops the boot-parameter attack.
LUKS alone is sufficient — encryption solves physical access entirely.
Remove the GRUB menu timeout so attackers can't see the menu.
scenarios.why: A GRUB password prevents editing boot entries (blocking the init=/bin/bash trick) but does nothing if the attacker pulls the disk — that's LUKS's job. Conversely LUKS doesn't stop someone from booting your running system into a root shell if the volume is already unlocked at boot. Physical-access defense needs both layers.
scenarios.hint: Two different attacks: editing the boot entry, and stealing the disk. Does one control stop both?

scenarios.title: Network team says it's the server
scenarios.situation: Users report an app is unreachable. The network team insists the network is fine and blames your RHEL server. You need to prove where the break is — host firewall, service state, or actual network.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct isolation sequence?
evidence:
$ ss -tlnp | grep 8443
(empty)
$ systemctl is-active myapp
active
$ firewall-cmd --list-ports
8443/tcp
choices: The service is 'active' but nothing listens on 8443 — the app failed to bind (check journalctl); the firewall is correctly open and the network is likely innocent. Diagnose the bind failure first.
Open more firewall ports — the network team is probably wrong about the firewall.
Reboot the server; that resolves most network disputes.
Ask the network team to check again — the firewall shows 8443/tcp open so it must be their problem.
scenarios.why: Isolation order: is the process listening (ss) → is the service healthy (systemctl/journalctl) → is the host firewall permitting (firewall-cmd) → then the network. Here ss shows no listener despite 'active' status — the app likely crashed its listener thread or misconfigured its bind address. The firewall is already correct; rebooting destroys evidence.
scenarios.hint: 'Active' doesn't mean 'listening'. Which command shows whether anyone is actually accepting connections on 8443?

domains.name: RHEL Storage, SELinux & Containers
domains.summary: RHCSA-weighted RHEL skills: dnf modules, SELinux contexts and booleans, Stratis storage, NFS, rootless Podman with systemd, and time sync. Independent training content; this course confers no certificate.

scenarios.title: The Wrong Node.js
scenarios.situation: `dnf install nodejs` gives v16 but the app needs v20. The repo clearly has newer versions — `dnf module list nodejs` shows several streams.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct dnf move?
choices: `dnf module reset nodejs && dnf module enable nodejs:20 && dnf install nodejs` — modules version-lock streams; you must switch the enabled stream before installing
`dnf update nodejs`; updates follow the newest stream automatically
Download the v20 RPM by hand and `rpm -i`; modules are optional
Enable all streams at once; dnf picks the newest
scenarios.why: Modular repos isolate major versions into streams — installing without switching streams pins you to the default. reset+enable+install is the supported stream switch; manual RPMs bypass dependency resolution and future updates.
scenarios.hint: What selects *which* major version dnf considers?

scenarios.title: Moved Files, Silent Denials
scenarios.situation: A web directory moved from `/root/site` to `/var/www/site` serves 403s. Permissions are 755, ownership correct — but AVC denials fill the audit log.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct SELinux fix?
evidence: avc: denied { getattr } for httpd, tcontext=admin_home_t
choices: `restorecon -Rv /var/www/site` — moved files keep their old context; restorecon reapplies the policy's default contexts (`httpd_sys_content_t`) for the new path
`setenforce 0`; SELinux is blocking a legitimate move
`chcon -t httpd_sys_content_t` on every file — but remember it won't survive a relabel
Move the files back to /root; web content must live in home directories
scenarios.why: `mv` preserves contexts — files created under /root carry admin_home_t forever. restorecon applies the file-context database (persistent across relabels); chcon is a temporary manual override. setenforce 0 disables the protection instead of fixing the label.
scenarios.hint: What remembers the *correct* label for a path: the file, or the policy database?

scenarios.title: Pool It Like It's 2026
scenarios.situation: Two new disks must become one thin-provisioned, snapshot-capable pool for `/data` — without hand-managing LVM thin pools.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct RHEL-native approach?
choices: Stratis: `stratis pool create datapool /dev/sdc /dev/sdd`, `stratis filesystem create datapool datafs`, mount the UUID — thin provisioning and snapshots without manual thin-pool math
Classic LVM thin pools; Stratis is just a wrapper with no benefit
RAID0 the disks and format ext4; pooling is overkill
Use btrfs; it's the RHEL default
scenarios.why: Stratis is RHEL's answer to simplified pooled storage: thin provisioning, snapshots, and cache tiers managed declaratively. Manual thin-pool LVM works but demands careful metadata sizing; btrfs is not the RHEL default (XFS is).
scenarios.hint: Which tool gives pooled, thin-provisioned storage with the least manual math?

scenarios.title: Mounts That Survive Reboot
scenarios.situation: An NFS share must mount at boot on 30 app servers, but a dead NFS server currently hangs every boot for 90 seconds.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct resilient mount?
evidence: boot hangs 90s when nfs01 is down
choices: Use automount (`autofs`) or systemd `.automount` units with `x-systemd.automount` — the share mounts on first access and boot never blocks on it; keep `_netdev` so ordering is network-aware
Add `nofail` to fstab and accept the 90s hang as normal
Mount it in rc.local after boot completes
Switch to hard-coded IP mounts; DNS is the hang
scenarios.why: automount mounts on demand — a down server delays only first access, never the boot. `_netdev` tells systemd the mount needs networking. nofail skips the mount but the boot still waits on the timeout.
scenarios.hint: What mounts the share only when someone actually uses it?

scenarios.title: Containers That Outlive the Login
scenarios.situation: A rootless Podman container must start at boot and restart on failure — but it was launched from a user shell and dies at logout.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct RHEL approach?
evidence: podman run -d ... (from user shell; dies at logout)
choices: Generate a systemd user unit (`podman generate systemd --new --name app > ~/.config/systemd/user/app.service`, or write a Quadlet `.container` file), then `loginctl enable-linger user` + `systemctl --user enable --now app` — linger keeps user services alive across logouts and boots
Run the container as root; rootless containers can't be services
Add `podman start` to the user's `.bash_profile`
Use Docker instead; Podman can't do services
scenarios.why: Quadlet/systemd user units are the RHEL-native way to run rootless containers as managed services; `enable-linger` is the key that lets user units run at boot without a login session. Root containers for app workloads violate least privilege.
scenarios.hint: What lets a *user* systemd unit run when nobody is logged in?

scenarios.title: Five Minutes Into the Future
scenarios.situation: Kerberos auth and TLS keep failing on one host; its clock is 5 minutes ahead of the domain. `ntpd` isn't installed.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct time sync fix?
evidence: NTP service: inactive; clock skew +5min vs DC
kinit: clock skew too great; TLS handshake failures
choices: Enable chrony: `systemctl enable --now chronyd` with the domain NTP servers in `/etc/chrony.conf` — Kerberos tolerates ~5 minutes of skew max, and chrony is RHEL's default NTP implementation
Run `date -s` to set the clock manually; one-time fixes hold
Install ntpd; chrony is deprecated on RHEL
Increase Kerberos' allowed skew to 30 minutes; time sync is optional
scenarios.why: Kerberos and TLS both depend on accurate time (default max skew 5 minutes). chrony is RHEL's supported NTP client — it slews the clock smoothly instead of stepping. Manual `date -s` drifts again within days; widening the skew tolerance weakens replay protection.
scenarios.hint: Which security protocols break first when clocks disagree?

lessons.title: RHCSA — Core concepts
concepts: systemd is the init system: 'systemctl start/stop' changes the now, 'systemctl enable/disable' changes what happens at boot, and 'systemctl status' shows both plus recent log lines.
Storage on RHEL is layered — disk, partition or PV, volume group, logical volume, filesystem — and each layer has its own tool (lsblk, pvs/vgs/lvs, mkfs, mount), so diagnose at the right layer.
firewalld manages the host firewall through zones and services; '--permanent' writes config and '--reload' applies it, while runtime-only changes vanish on reload.

SELinux enforces mandatory access control by type: processes run in domains (httpd_t) and files carry types (httpd_sys_content_t); denials are diagnosed with ausearch and fixed with semanage fcontext + restorecon.
Podman runs OCI containers daemonless and rootless by default on RHEL; rootless containers cannot bind privileged ports (<1024) or access host devices without explicit delegation.
User and group management (useradd, usermod, groupadd) is file-based in /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /etc/group — understand the files and the tools become obvious.

example.code:
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=http
sudo firewall-cmd --reload
sudo firewall-cmd --list-services
example.walkthrough: The first command writes the http service into the permanent configuration of the active zone. '--reload' applies permanent config to the runtime without dropping connections. The last command confirms http is now listed.

pitfalls: Common trap: editing unit files under /usr/lib/systemd/system — they are package-owned and your changes vanish on update; use 'systemctl edit' for drop-ins.
Common trap: using chcon for an SELinux labeling fix — it works until the next relabel; semanage fcontext is the persistent fix.
Common trap: forgetting '--permanent' on firewall-cmd — the rule works until the next reload, then silently disappears.
Common trap: extending a logical volume but forgetting to grow the filesystem (xfs_growfs / resize2fs) — the space stays invisible to df.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: RHCSA Spine — Core concepts
concepts: Boot is a chain — firmware, GRUB2, kernel, systemd: each stage's success is visible on the console, so localize failures by finding the last stage that completed.
systemd targets (rescue, multi-user, graphical) are synchronization points; 'systemd.unit=' on the kernel command line boots into any of them for recovery.
LVM separates physical disks (PVs) from usable space (VGs) from filesystems (LVs): extend at each layer in order, and use snapshots for instant pre-change rollback points.
XFS (RHEL default) grows online but never shrinks — 'lvextend -r' handles LV plus filesystem in one step; ext4 uses resize2fs and can do both.
Linux routing is longest-match: connected subnet routes beat defaults, and a host should have exactly one default gateway — a second default is a classic post-reboot breakage.
Troubleshoot in isolation order: process listening (ss), service state and logs (systemctl, journalctl), host firewall (firewall-cmd), then the network — prove each layer before blaming the next.

example.walkthrough: Extends the logical volume by 10 GB and, via -r, grows the filesystem online in the same command. df confirms the new space is visible; lvs shows the LV's new size. No unmount, no downtime.

pitfalls: Common trap: growing the LV but not the filesystem — df won't show new space until xfs_growfs/resize2fs runs; '-r' prevents this.
Common trap: shrinking XFS — impossible; plan LV sizes accordingly or use ext4 where shrink is needed.
Common trap: two default gateways after adding a NIC — remove the spurious one; connected routes already cover the local subnet.
Common trap: editing fstab with device names (/dev/sdb1) — names shift; use UUIDs from blkid.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

labs.title: Harden a fresh RHEL host: services and firewall
labs.objective: Enable only required services at boot and expose exactly one application port through firewalld.
steps: List enabled services with 'systemctl list-unit-files --state=enabled' and identify anything unnecessary.
Disable and stop one unneeded service with 'systemctl disable --now <service>'.
Enable the application service persistently: 'systemctl enable --now myapp'.
Add its port permanently: 'firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=8443/tcp' then 'firewall-cmd --reload'.
Verify with 'systemctl is-enabled myapp' and 'firewall-cmd --list-ports'.

checks.hint: List the open ports in the active zone.

labs.title: Relocate a web root under SELinux
labs.objective: Move a document root to a nonstandard path and make it serve correctly with SELinux enforcing.
steps: Create /srv/www, place an index.html, and confirm 403s with SELinux enforcing.
Read the denial with 'ausearch -m avc -ts recent' and note the wrong file type with 'ls -Z'.
Declare the correct type: 'semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/srv/www(/.*)?"'.
Apply it: 'restorecon -Rv /srv/www' and verify with 'ls -Z'.
Confirm the page serves and that 'getenforce' still reports Enforcing.

labs.title: LVM lifecycle: extend and snapshot
labs.objective: Extend a logical volume online and practice snapshot-based rollback.
steps: Inspect the stack: 'pvs', 'vgs', 'lvs', and 'lsblk -f' to map PV→VG→LV→filesystem.
Extend an LV: 'lvextend -r -L +2G <lv-path>' and verify with 'df -h'.
Create a snapshot: 'lvcreate -s -n snap_test -L 1G <lv-path>'.
Write a canary file, then 'lvconvert --merge' the snapshot (after unmount if required) to roll back.
Verify the canary file is gone and remove leftover snapshots.

checks.hint: List logical volumes to see the snapshot.

labs.title: Diagnose a broken boot entry
labs.objective: Practice GRUB-level recovery by booting to rescue target and fixing a bad fstab.
steps: In a test VM, add a bogus entry to /etc/fstab (nonexistent UUID) and reboot.
At the GRUB menu, press 'e', add 'systemd.unit=rescue.target' to the linux line, boot with Ctrl-X.
In the rescue shell, run 'blkid' and correct the fstab entry.
Run 'systemctl daemon-reload' then 'systemctl default' to continue booting.
Confirm clean boot and remove the practice entry.

checks.hint: Check the current target while in rescue mode.

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about the most technically difficult problem you have run into — a homelab, a broken environment, anything — and how you solved it.
points: Pick ONE problem with a real evidence trail: the symptom, what you measured, the hypothesis you tested
Show the loop: scope, observe, hypothesize, smallest safe change, validate — interviewers score the method, not just the fix
Name the tools (VM build, networking, logs) and the lesson it taught you
Close with the result in concrete terms: what works now that did not before
pitfalls: Choosing a story with no real obstacle (“I Googled it” is not a story)
Skipping validation — saying it worked without proving it
Rambling past two minutes without reaching the result

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you dealt with a frustrated customer or user while something was broken.
points: Lead with empathy and ownership: acknowledge the impact before the technical detail
Show translation: what you told them, in their language, plus the timeline you committed to
Show judgment: the narrow fix you chose and what you refused to do (e.g., disabling the control to clear the symptom)
Close with the relationship outcome, not just the technical one
pitfalls: Badmouthing the customer to sound decisive
Promising a timeline you could not keep
Framing the user as the problem rather than the situation

points: Connect prevention to something concrete: a moment you saw detection arrive too late, or a system you hardened
Tie their model to your instincts: deny-by-default matches how you already think about trust
Show service orientation: the Cyber Hero culture rewards the 2 a.m. helper — give an example of being one
Name one forward-looking reason: Zero Trust, the MSP mission, or the bootcamp community investment
pitfalls: Generic flattery with no specifics about the company
Leading with compensation, title, or location convenience
Claiming expertise in products you have only read about — frame it as studied, not mastered
Staying vague ('I analyzed the data') instead of naming what you connected.
Skipping your own role: what did YOU see that others missed?
No outcome: what changed because you joined the dots?
points: The scattered signals and why nobody had connected them yet
The specific links you drew between them (shared host, time, infrastructure)
What the bigger picture turned out to be and what action it drove
What the experience taught you about investigating
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you connected scattered clues into a bigger picture that others had missed.

pitfalls: Claiming you fixed everything: credibility comes from trade-offs, not heroics.
Hiding the constraint: the limitation is what makes the prioritization story real.
No metric: 'better' needs a before-and-after.
points: The constraint (time, budget, staff) and the size of the backlog
How you decided what mattered most (what was reachable, what was critical)
What you did first and what you deliberately deferred
The measurable result of the prioritization
behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to prioritize risks or fixes with limited time or resources. How did you decide what came first?

pitfalls: Reciting jargon to a non-technical audience and calling it communication.
Skipping the audience's reaction: did they actually understand and act?
Making yourself the hero instead of the translator.
points: The technical finding and why it mattered
Who the audience was and what they cared about
How you reframed it (a picture, an analogy, a story)
What decision or action the audience took because they understood
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you explained a complex technical finding to a non-technical audience and it changed a decision.
Tell me about a time you used automation or AI to solve a security problem.
points: The repetitive security task and what it cost in analyst time
The automation or AI approach you built and how you validated it
Measured outcome: time saved, detection gained, false positives changed
pitfalls: Describing the tool but never the validation
No measurable outcome

behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to decide whether to trust an automated security decision.
points: The stakes of the automated action and its blast radius
How you verified before acting (or the gate you built)
What happened and what you would automate differently next time
pitfalls: Saying you always trust the tool
No mention of blast radius or reversibility

items: Founded 2017 in Orlando, FL — Danny Jenkins (CEO), Sami Jenkins (COO), John Carolan (QA)
Philosophy: deny-by-default / default-deny — approve known-good, deny the rest
Customers: 70,000+ organizations, sold heavily through the MSP channel

sections.heading: Product stack
items: Allowlisting — default-deny execution control for apps, DLLs, scripts, installers
Ringfencing — constrains allowed apps: app-to-app, file, registry, network
Storage Control — USB/device policy by serial, user, file type, encryption
Elevation Control — just-in-time per-app admin, no standing rights
Network Control — host firewall; port/IP/dynamic-ACL rules; ZTNA foundation
Web Control — agent-based DNS/URL category filtering, works off-network
Cyber Hero MDR — 24/7/365 US-based response, ~60-second average
Testing Environment — one-button VDI sandbox; checks AV flags, canary files, registry changes

sections.heading: Rule strength (strongest to weakest)
items: Certificate/publisher rules — survive version updates
Hash rules — precise but break on every new version
Path rules — weakest; never in user-writable locations
Learning Mode catalogs before enforcement; Installation Mode pauses blocking — scope and time-box both

sections.heading: Terminal evidence commands
items: nmap <host> — which ports answer (22/80/443 open)
dig <name> — ANSWER SECTION with the A record
ss — listening sockets
systemctl status <svc> — unit state
journalctl -u <svc> — service logs
sha256sum <file> — real SHA-256 identity
grep <pattern> <file> — search the record
ps — what is actually running

sections.heading: Graph vocabulary
items: node — any entity tracked in the model (user, host, IP, domain, file hash, vulnerability)
edge — a labeled relationship between two nodes (logged into, resolved to, downloaded)
degree — number of edges on a node; high-degree nodes are attacker highways
centrality — how much traffic or how many paths flow through a node
directed edge — a relationship with a direction (A downloaded FROM B)
security graph — the living model of your whole environment as nodes and edges
attack graph — the subgraph of exploitable paths to your targets
knowledge graph — threat-intel indicators linked to campaigns and actors

sections.heading: Attack-graph playbook
items: inventory first — you cannot graph what you have not discovered
model flaws AND misconfigs as exploit edges
compute shortest paths to the crown jewels
find the choke point (highest betweenness on those paths)
break the path: patch, segment, or remove the edge
re-scan and re-run the graph to prove the path is gone
never trust yesterday's graph — redeployments redraw the map

sections.heading: Zero Trust + graphs
items: never trust, always verify — re-evaluate every access decision
assume breach — treat unexpected edges as hostile until proven otherwise
microsegmentation — allow-list approved edges, alert on new ones
ReBAC — policies are path queries on the identity graph
continuous verification — device/location/behavior edges change, trust follows
anomalous edge — a first-seen connection between strangers is the classic signal

sections.heading: ML detection vocabulary
items: Supervised learning — learns from labeled examples; strong on known threats, blind to novel ones
Unsupervised learning — finds structure without labels; clustering and dimensionality reduction
Anomaly detection — models 'normal' and flags deviations; the workhorse for novel threats
UEBA — user and entity behavior analytics: per-user baselines plus peer-group comparison
Feature engineering — encoding raw logs into model inputs (login velocity, rare processes, domain entropy)
Concept drift — model decay as attacker behavior and legitimate traffic shift over time

sections.heading: Detection metrics
items: Precision — of all flagged alerts, how many were real
Recall — of all real attacks, how many were flagged
Threshold tuning — sliding the decision cutoff trades precision against recall
Alert fatigue — when false positives train analysts to ignore the queue
DGA — domain generation algorithm; detected via character entropy of domain names

sections.heading: Agent and LLM security
items: Direct prompt injection — attacker input overrides app instructions (OWASP LLM01:2025, the #1 LLM risk)
Indirect prompt injection — hidden instructions inside retrieved data (email, web, docs)
Jailbreak — defeating the model's own safety policy; distinct from hijacking app behavior
Tool poisoning — malicious tool descriptions or metadata steer an agent to misuse its tools (MCP ecosystem risk)
Insecure output handling — executing or trusting model output without validation
Least-privilege tools — grant each tool only the scope its task requires

sections.heading: Adversarial ML and governance
items: Evasion — perturbing inputs at inference time to dodge a classifier
Poisoning — corrupting training data to corrupt the model
Extraction — querying a model to steal its behavior or parameters
MITRE ATLAS — knowledge base of adversarial ML tactics and techniques
Red-teaming and evals — adversarial testing of AI systems before deployment
Human-in-the-loop — required approval for high-impact or irreversible agent actions
SOAR — security orchestration, automation and response; automate enrichment, gate containment

glossary.def: Default-deny execution control: only explicitly approved applications, scripts, and installers may run.
Default-allow model: everything runs except recognized-bad items — the window zero-days live in.
Deny-by-default posture: unknown code, devices, or connections are refused unless explicitly approved.
Containment applied on top of allowlisting; restricts what a permitted app may do across app-to-app, file, registry, and network dimensions.
Agent mode that catalogs applications and dependencies and auto-builds policies before enforcement; temporarily disables file blocking.
Temporary mode that pauses file blocking for installs — must be tightly scoped and time-boxed.
Grants specific approved applications admin rights for standard users — just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed — without standing admin rights.
An elevated or trusted process spawning another tool (e.g., PowerShell) to inherit its privileges — countered by ringfencing the elevated process.
Device and path policy: USB approved by serial, user, file type, time, and encryption; unapproved devices do not connect.
Centrally managed host firewall; rules by port, source IP, and dynamic ACLs; egress allowlisting pins apps to approved destinations.
Zero Trust Network Access: per-session, per-application brokered connections (commonly over port 443) with no open inbound ports — deny-by-default for network access.
Portal queue where end-user software requests arrive for admin review and decision.
Real-time audit showing what was allowed or denied across endpoints — and why; the evidence layer for triage.
One-button cloud VDI sandbox launched from an approval request; logs AV flags, canary-file access, and registry/system changes.
24/7/365 US-based managed detection and response team; validates alerts, isolates hosts, acts on customer runbooks; ~60-second average response.
Design and operate as if the attacker already has a foothold — least privilege, containment, and monitoring everywhere.
Attacks that hijack trusted built-in tools (Word, PowerShell) instead of dropping malware — defeated by behavior containment, not signatures.
Scoped, ticketed, tested changes with validation and rollback — emergency speed never cancels the process.
A node in an attack graph representing a system or weakness, connected by edges that represent steps an attacker could take between them.
How central a node is to paths through the graph (for example, betweenness: how many shortest paths cross it).
The most valuable assets in the environment (customer data, finance systems, source code): what attack paths are measured against.
A labeled connection between two nodes, representing a relationship such as 'logged into' or 'resolved to'.
A graph of threat indicators (IPs, domains, hashes) linked to campaigns, actors, and each other through shared infrastructure.
The practice of mapping relationships in data to reveal hidden associations; rooted in Euler's 1736 graph theory, 1970s paper link charts, and post-2001 intelligence work.
A segment of the network so small that its allowed communications can be enumerated as a graph of approved edges.
An entity in the graph: a user, host, IP address, domain, file, or vulnerability.
Access control where policy is evaluated by traversing relationships on a graph (for example: user reports_to manager who owns the resource's project).
A machine-learning model that operates directly on graph structure to classify nodes or subgraphs, for example labeling attack vs normal behavior.
Monitoring user and entity behavior by modeling their normal relationship patterns and flagging structural anomalies.
ML trained on labeled examples; classifies new inputs into known categories.
ML approach that models normal behavior and flags statistically rare deviations.
Turning raw telemetry into numeric model inputs, e.g. login velocity or domain entropy.
Share of flagged alerts that were real; the false-positive economics of the queue.
Share of real attacks the detector flagged; the miss rate's complement.
Decay of model performance as the data distribution shifts over time.
Attacker-crafted instructions that override an LLM application's intended behavior; direct (user input) or indirect (retrieved data).
Crafted input that defeats an LLM's own safety policy or refusal behavior.
Malicious tool descriptions or metadata that manipulate an AI agent into misusing its tools.
Failing to validate LLM output before acting on it, e.g. executing generated commands.
Adversarial ML technique: perturbing inputs to cross a classifier's decision boundary.
Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems; MITRE's knowledge base of AI attack tactics.
Security orchestration, automation and response; playbooks that enrich automatically and gate containment on humans.
Required human approval before high-impact or irreversible automated actions.

Two STAR stories ready: hardest technical problem; a frustrated customer or user

Ringfencing explained in one plain-English sentence (the Word-on-a-leash version)

Three questions to ask them: team on-call shape, approval SLA expectations, what “most helpful” looks like on the team
Logistics: 1901 Summit Tower Blvd, Orlando FL; in-office role; ID and references ready
Define your crown jewels before you model anything.
Build the asset-and-access graph from live sources (scans, configs, identity), not from the CMDB alone.
Model vulnerabilities AND misconfigurations as exploit edges.
Compute shortest attack paths to each crown jewel; name the choke points.
Prioritize remediation by path risk, not by raw severity score.
Express at least one access policy as a relationship path (ReBAC pilot).
Baseline approved communication edges per segment; alert on first-seen edges.
Brief the next incident or risk review with the graph, not a spreadsheet.
